name: Cinoxate
lead: Cinoxate is an organic UVB filter, an ester of methoxycinnamic acid and 2-ethoxyethanol, used in some sunscreen formulations.[1] According to Wikipedia, the US FDA approved it as a UV filter in 1961, and a 2023 review cited there describes it as no longer commonly used in cosmetic formulations.[1]

Published research on cinoxate is sparse. A 1989 laboratory study found it increased chromosome-level changes in cultured hamster cells exposed to certain damaging agents, and a 2024 computational study flagged it as a possible PPAR-gamma agonist; neither involved human use.[2][3]

paras: Cinoxate has a molar mass of about 250 g/mol and is a slightly yellow, viscous, water-insoluble liquid that mixes with alcohols, esters and vegetable oils.[1] It belongs to the cinnamate family, a group of derivatives widely used in cosmetics for functions that include UV absorption.[4]

Cinoxate has been used as a UVB filter in sunscreens and is grouped with other cinnamates such as octyl methoxycinnamate.[1] The FDA approved it in 1961, and a 2023 review described it as not commonly used in cosmetics now.[1]

In a 1989 study, cinoxate enhanced sister-chromatid exchanges and chromosome aberrations induced by other agents in cultured Chinese hamster ovary cells.[2] A 2024 cheminformatic analysis predicted cinoxate to act as an obesogenic PPAR-gamma agonist, a computational finding that the authors framed as requiring further testing.[3]
No studies found. Related research is limited to cell-culture and computational work.[2][3]

timeline.event: US FDA approves cinoxate as a UV filter.[1]

card.summary: An older cinnamate UVB filter, approved in the US in 1961 and now rarely used.
card.note: Little modern research; only cell-culture and computational safety findings exist.

quick.overview:
Cinoxate is a cinnamate-based UVB filter that the US FDA approved in 1961. It appeared in some older sunscreens.

A 2023 review cited by Wikipedia describes it as no longer commonly used in cosmetics.
quick.mechanism: As a cinnamate ester, it absorbs ultraviolet B light in the skin's surface layers.
quick.risks: No human safety trials are documented in the sources. A 1989 cell study reported increased chromosome changes when combined with other agents, and a 2024 computational study predicted PPAR-gamma activity.
